opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's one of the hardest questions in research management, and I think the honest answer is that you can't evaluate it purely on outcomes. If you only reward the bets that pay off, you train everyone to stop making bets, and then you've lost the thing that actually moves the field forward.

So the first thing I look at is the quality of the reasoning going in. Was this a well-posed bet? Did the person have a clear hypothesis, a sense of why it might work when others thought it wouldn't, and a sense of what success would even look like? A bet that fails for good reasons is very different from a bet that was poorly framed from the start.

The second thing is how they fail. Good researchers fail fast and fail informatively. They design experiments so that even a negative result tells you something: this direction is closed, here's why, here's what we learned about the problem. If someone spends six months and comes back with "it didn't work" and no real understanding of why, that's a concern. If they come back with a crisp picture of the failure and that picture changes how the rest of the team thinks, that's real value, even if it never shows up as a headline result.

Third, I look at whether they're updating. Repeated failure isn't necessarily bad, but repeated failure on the same underlying mistake is. Are they taking what they learned and making sharper bets, or are they just rerolling the dice?

And then there's a portfolio view. At the organizational level you want some fraction of people working on things with low odds and huge upside. You expect most of those to fail. That's the deal. So part of my job is making sure the person isn't carrying all that risk alone, that they have some steadier work alongside it so their whole career doesn't ride on one coin flip.

Eventually, though, you do need some signal. If it's been years and there's been no traction and no insight that's helped anyone else, it's fair to have a candid conversation. Usually that conversation isn't "you're bad at this." It's more like, let's look at your instincts together and figure out where they're well calibrated and where they aren't. A lot of the best researchers I know went through a stretch like that, and what got them out of it was someone helping them recalibrate rather than giving up on them.

r001.rationale: It says to assess the quality of the reasoning and whether each bet was well framed, with a clear hypothesis and rationale, distinguishing sound bets that fail from poorly framed ones.

r002.rationale: It argues for evaluating more than outcomes and recognizing informative failures and high-upside work, but does not state that occasional valuable successes justify repeated failed bets.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is one of the hardest things about running a research org, honestly. Because the whole premise of a research lab is that you want people taking bets that have a real chance of failing. If everyone's succeeding all the time, that's actually a signal that nobody's being ambitious enough.

But at the same time, you can't just say "failure is fine" and leave it there, because then you have no way to distinguish between someone who's taking smart risks and someone who's just not executing. So the way I think about it is, I try to separate the outcome from the process.

The first thing I look at is: was the bet well-reasoned going in? Did they have a clear hypothesis, a clear sense of why this might work and what the world would look like if it did? Or was it more of a vibe? Because if the thesis was sound and it just didn't pan out, that's often just what research is. Nature doesn't owe you a result.

The second thing, and this is maybe the more important one, is: what did they learn, and how fast did they learn it? A good researcher whose bet fails should come out of it with a very sharp understanding of why it failed. And ideally that understanding becomes useful to the rest of the org. Some of our most important decisions have come from negative results, where someone ran the experiment, it didn't work, and that saved ten other people from going down the same path. That's a real contribution even though there's no paper and no headline.

The third thing is whether they kill things at the right time. There's a failure mode where someone falls in love with an idea and keeps pouring compute and months into it well past the point where the evidence was telling them to stop. That's different from a bet failing. That's a judgment problem. So I pay a lot of attention to how people respond to disconfirming evidence. Do they update, or do they rationalize?

And then honestly, I look at the trajectory. Someone who's failed three times but each time the bets got sharper, the hypotheses got more specific, they're reading the field better, that's someone I want to keep betting on. Someone whose fourth failure looks exactly like their first, that's a different conversation.

The last thing I'd say is, you have to be careful about what you incentivize. If people see that the folks who get promoted are the ones who took the safe, incremental path and shipped something, then everyone will do that, and you'll have a very productive lab that never discovers anything. So part of my job is to make it visibly okay to have a bad year on a good bet. Not infinitely okay, but okay.

r001.rationale: The response says to assess whether the bet was well-reasoned, with a clear hypothesis and sound thesis, even if it failed.

r002.rationale: The response accepts failure on a good bet and values learning, but does not say that occasional sufficiently valuable successes can justify repeated failed bets.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to separate the outcome of a bet from the quality of the judgment that went into it. If you want people to take genuinely high-risk bets, some of those have to fail. Otherwise, you’re implicitly asking everyone to work on things that are pretty safe.

So I’d look at: Was there a compelling reason to try this? Did they identify the key uncertainty and design an experiment that could resolve it? And when the evidence came back negative, did they update quickly? A failed project can still be valuable if it tells the rest of the team, “This direction doesn’t work, and here’s why.”

But repeated failure isn’t automatically a badge of good research, either. You want to see their judgment improving. Are they finding more informative experiments? Are they incorporating what they learned into the next bet? I’d be much more concerned about someone repeating the same mistake or explaining away every negative result than someone whose ambitious ideas haven’t worked yet.

r001.rationale: The response evaluates the reasoning and experiments behind a bet, but does not clearly identify the soundness of the researcher’s ideas as a basis for evaluation.

r002.rationale: It says failed projects can provide useful information, but does not state that occasional valuable successes can justify repeated unsuccessful bets.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to separate the outcome of a bet from the quality of the thinking behind it. If you’re encouraging people to do high-risk research, some of those bets have to fail. Otherwise, you’re probably encouraging people to be too conservative.

So I’d look at: Was there a compelling reason to try this? Did they design experiments that could actually tell them whether the idea was working? And when the evidence came back negative, did they update? A failed project can still be valuable if it teaches the team something and changes what we do next.

But repeated failure does warrant a conversation. Are they getting better at choosing bets? Are they finding cheaper, faster ways to test their assumptions? You want to give people room to pursue something uncertain while still expecting good judgment and learning along the way.

r001.rationale: The response says to assess the quality of the thinking behind a bet, including whether there was a compelling reason to try it and whether the researcher learned from evidence.

r002.rationale: It says some high-risk bets are expected to fail and that failures can teach the team, but does not say that occasional valuable successes justify repeated failures.
